classification.habit: Bulbous perennial herb, commonly cultivated as an annual
classification.distribution: Widely cultivated worldwide; common in India

identification.description: Bulbous herb with linear flat leaves, an underground compound bulb and a characteristic strong odour.
identification.whole_plant: Herb arising from a compound bulb with several narrow leaves.
identification.root: Fibrous roots arise from the basal plate of the bulb.
identification.stem: Short compressed basal stem; a flowering scape may arise centrally.
identification.leaf: Long, flat, linear to strap-shaped leaves with sheathing bases.
identification.flower: Small whitish flowers borne in a rounded umbel; bulbils may occur in the inflorescence.
identification.fruit: Fruiting is uncommon in cultivated garlic; reproductive structures may include bulbils.
identification.seed: True seed production is uncommon in many cultivated forms; cloves are vegetative propagules, not seeds.
identification_points: Bulbils/umbel on flowering scape in suitable material

therapeutics.precautions: Strongly pungent material may cause gastrointestinal irritation in some people; use appropriate clinical references.

classical_reference.shloka_reference_status: source-hub-added; exact verse/edition requires text-level verification
reference_hubs: TDU Indian Medicinal Plants Database — Shlokas

major_constituents: Allicin and related organosulfur compounds formed during tissue disruption
phytochemistry.chemical_notes: Garlic chemistry changes rapidly after crushing because alliinase converts alliin to thiosulfinates such as allicin.

modern_information.evidence_summary: Garlic has been extensively studied for cardiovascular, metabolic and antimicrobial-related effects. Study outcomes depend on preparation, dose and population and are not reproduced here as guaranteed therapeutic effects.
modern_information.safety_notes: Garlic may increase bleeding tendency in some settings and can cause gastrointestinal irritation; review concurrent medicines when clinically relevant.

viva_questions: What is the useful part of Rasona?
How is a garlic bulb different from a true seed?
mnemonics: Rasona = Lashuna = remember the pungent compound bulb.
student.quick_revision: Rasona (Allium sativum): bulbous Amaryllidaceae herb; bulb/cloves are used; flat leaves and strong odour are characteristic; alliin/allicin chemistry is important.

teaching_points: Demonstrate bulb, cloves and basal plate.
Explain enzymatic formation of allicin after crushing.
practical_points: Compare fresh intact bulb with crushed material for odour.

doctor.quick_reference: Rasona is traditionally used mainly as bulb in Vata-related and digestive contexts; dosing requires a verified reference.
key_precautions: Review anticoagulant/antiplatelet medicines when clinically relevant
